name: Beef organ / beef juice extract

lead: These are products made from beef organs or concentrated beef extract, sold as capsules or food-style supplements. Users take them as a dense source of protein and micronutrients to support training, recovery and a stronger physique. Meat extract dates to Liebig in 1840, and offal is a traditional food in many cuisines.

The chain is concentrated protein and micronutrients, better recovery, then more muscle and a leaner build. The case rests mainly on general nutrition knowledge about meat and offal; no trial of a branded organ or juice supplement for muscle was found, though a small registered study looked at absorption of hydrolysed beef.

paras: People take organ capsules or beef-extract products daily alongside a high-protein diet, or eat liver and other offal as whole food. It is used as a background nutrition habit, so changes are judged over weeks to months of training.

Sold as food or supplement. Older lab studies found mutagenic compounds forming in cooked beef and beef extract; the relevance to modern products is not established. Those who need to limit certain nutrients for medical reasons should check with a clinician.

angle.text: Beef organ and beef juice products are used as nutrient-dense support so you can recover well and build a stronger, leaner physique. The case comes from general nutrition knowledge about meat and offal; product-specific trials on muscle were not found.

lead: Beef organ and beef juice or meat extract supplements are concentrated products derived from cattle meat or offal, sold as nutrient-dense foods or capsules for muscle, energy and general health. Offal means the internal organs of a butchered animal, and these are eaten in many cuisines.[1] Meat extract is a concentrated stock first developed commercially in the nineteenth century.[2]

People use them as a route to better physiques and skin. The chain described in fitness and looksmaxxing circles runs from nutrient-dense food (liver in particular is rich in vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin and iron) to better energy and training capacity, and in turn to more muscle and a leaner look.[3][4] Wikipedia notes that offal intake has grown in some countries, partly promoted by fitness influencers.[1]

No published trial reviewed here tests a branded organ or beef-juice capsule for muscle or appearance outcomes. A small registered study has examined the absorption and muscle-stimulating effect of hydrolysed minced beef,[5] and other registered trials look at whole beef in contexts such as ageing muscle.[6] Reference works also note that liver holds preformed vitamin A at levels that can be harmful if eaten daily.[3]
infobox: Fresh or frozen organ meat, desiccated capsules, meat extract
Meat extract (e.g. Bovril, Liebig's extract, Bonox)[2]
Preformed vitamin A, vitamin B12, iron, riboflavin, copper[3][4]
Preformed vitamin A in liver can reach harmful levels with daily intake[3]

paras: The category covers several different things: fresh organ meat such as liver, heart or kidney; freeze-dried or desiccated organ capsules sold as supplements; and beef juice or meat extract, which is a concentrated product made by boiling meat and reducing the stock.[2] Offal is defined as the internal organs and some other parts of a butchered animal, eaten in many cuisines either as everyday food or as a delicacy.[1]

Attitudes to offal vary: some cultures treat it as taboo while others eat it daily. Regional dishes include haggis and black pudding in Britain, anticuchos in Peru, lampredotto in Italy and sundae in Korea.[1] Liver is eaten in many forms, from liver and onions in Britain to raw liver (asbeh nayeh) in Lebanon and tinned cod liver spreads in parts of Europe.[3]

Meat extract in the modern sense is mostly a flavouring. Current products such as Bovril combine beef stock, yeast extract and a small amount of dehydrated beef, and high-purity meat extract is also sold to laboratories for microbiology.[2] The capsule and powder products marketed to lifters are a separate, newer category that draws on the nutrient content of organs rather than on stock.

Liver is rich in protein and low in fat and carbohydrate, with very high levels of vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin and pantothenic acid and a large amount of iron; liver's B12 content helped lead to that vitamin's discovery.[3] Nutrient content varies by animal species.[3]

Looksmax.org posters present liver as a dense source of retinol, B12, copper and heme iron, and compare it with multivitamins. One long thread lists per-100 g figures for vitamin A, B12, copper, iron, folate and riboflavin and argues that the food form beats supplements.[4]

German chemist Justus von Liebig developed a concentrated beef extract in 1840, which he called Extractum carnis Liebig, as a cheaper substitute for meat; about 30 kg of meat made 1 kg of extract, which made it expensive.[2] Liebig's company opened a factory in Fray Bentos, Uruguay, in 1865, using meat from cattle raised for their hides at a third of British meat prices.[2] John Lawson Johnston created Johnston's Fluid Beef, later renamed Bovril, in the 1870s, adding flavourings that Liebig's extract lacked, and Bonox reached the Australian market in 1919, often served as a hot drink.[2]

Meat extracts have since been largely replaced by bouillon cubes and yeast extracts, though they remain an ingredient in some higher-end stock cubes.[2] The modern organ-meat supplement trend is tied more to ancestral-diet and fitness communities, where nose-to-tail eating is presented as a way to get micronutrients that muscle meat alone supplies in smaller amounts.[1][4]

In Ireland, Wikipedia reports that offal consumption has risen with growing awareness of its nutritional benefits, partly promoted by fitness influencers.[1] On looksmax.org, beef liver threads discuss raw versus cooked preparation, sourcing from non-industrial farms, and taste, with some users saying they eat it raw as a normal food from childhood and others describing it as unpleasant.[7][8]

T Nation threads discuss grass-fed and organic beef more broadly, with posters stating preferences for organically raised, pasture-fed or locally sourced meat, and organ meats come up in conversations about food preferences, where some members call them favourites and others describe them as hard to eat.[9][10][11]

Liver contains preformed vitamin A, which can reach harmful levels. One reference work states that a single 68 g slice of beef liver exceeds the tolerable upper intake for preformed vitamin A, notes that excess vitamin A in pregnancy has been linked to birth defects, and says daily consumption can be harmful.[3]

Separate 1970s and 1980s laboratory research reported that mutagenic compounds form when beef and beef extract are cooked, and that one such compound was carcinogenic in mice; the relevance of these findings to supplements has not been established.[12][13]

Raw consumption is a point of debate in forum threads. Posters on looksmax.org disagree over whether freezing is essential or undesirable, and the thread itself lists parasites among the topics it addresses.[4] Food-safety guidance for raw meat generally comes from public health agencies rather than from these communities.

A small registered study (about 10 participants) examined absorption and muscle-stimulating effects of hydrolysed and minced beef; its status is listed as unknown and no results are summarised.[5] Other registered trials examine ground beef or beef intake in contexts such as ageing muscle mass (12 participants, completed),[6] a lipoprotein metabolism study of ground beef (27 participants, completed),[14] and weight management (the Beef WISE study, 120 participants, completed),[15] but these concern whole beef rather than organ or juice supplements.

Further registrations include trials of habitual beef intake and brain-health markers (20 participants, recruiting)[16] and lean beef in adolescents with polycystic ovary syndrome (36 participants, recruiting),[17] as well as a beef-and-plant-burger metabolomics study.[18]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, beef liver is promoted by some posters as a nutritional staple, with disagreement about preparation.[4][7] On T Nation, beef is discussed mainly in terms of how it is raised.[9][10]
